en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 21.1 (SN 21.1, PTS SN ii 273) 1. Bhikkhuvagga Kolitasutta At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of four qualities, he is one who has reached the ultimate goal, the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate completion of the holy life; he is one who has laid down the burden, accomplished his own purpose, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, one completely liberated through final knowledge. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. Possessing these four qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has reached the ultimate goal, the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate completion of the holy life; he is one who has laid down the burden, accomplished his own purpose, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, one completely liberated through final knowledge. When this was said, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Koṭṭhita, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, you will not long remain without having attained what is far-reaching, of great fruit, and of a most sweet taste—that is, the four foundations of mindfulness. “What are the four? “Here, Koṭṭhita, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings... He dwells contemplating mind as mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. If you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, Koṭṭhita, you will not long remain without having attained what is far-reaching, of great fruit, and of a most sweet taste—that is, these four foundations of mindfulness. Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita became one of the arahants. Then, when the night was well advanced, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, it is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous how the meaning and the phrasing of the Blessed One’s words have been so well explained that they clarify the meaning. Just now, venerable sir, when I rose from my seat and paid homage to the Blessed One, I thought: ‘How many kinds of arahants are there in the world? “There are, Koṭṭhita, these five kinds of arahants in the world. What five? Here, Koṭṭhita, some person is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. This is the first kind of arahant in the world. Again, Koṭṭhita, some person is a once-returner, who, having returned to this world once more, will make an end of suffering. This is the second kind of arahant in the world. Again, Koṭṭhita, some person is a non-returner, who, having entirely transcended the plane of sense-sphere existence, will attain final nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. This is the third kind of arahant in the world. Again, Koṭṭhita, some person attains the cessation of perception and feeling. This is the fourth kind of arahant in the world. Again, Koṭṭhita, some person here attains the destruction of the taints. This is the fifth kind of arahant in the world. These, Koṭṭhita, are the five kinds of arahants in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous how the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma step by step, starting from the beginning, for the benefit of those who are later comers. For, venerable sir, when I rose from my seat and paid homage to the Blessed One, I thought: ‘How many kinds of arahants are there in the world? “It is wonderful, Koṭṭhita, it is marvelous how the meaning and the phrasing of the Blessed One’s words have been so well explained that they clarify the meaning. Just now, venerable sir, when I rose from my seat and paid homage to the Blessed One, I thought: ‘How many kinds of arahants are there in the world? “Koṭṭhita, if anyone should say: ‘I do not acknowledge any other ascetic or brahmin who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination,’ that would be a true statement. If anyone should say: ‘I do not acknowledge any other ascetic or brahmin who is a once-returner, who, having returned to this world once more, will make an end of suffering,’ that would be a true statement. If anyone should say: ‘I do not acknowledge any other ascetic or brahmin who is a non-returner, who, having entirely transcended the plane of sense-sphere existence, will attain final nibbāna there without ever returning from that world,’ that would be a true statement. If anyone should say: ‘I do not acknowledge any other ascetic or brahmin who attains the cessation of perception and feeling,’ that would be a true statement. If anyone should say: ‘I do not acknowledge any other ascetic or brahmin who has attained the destruction of the taints,’ that would be a true statement. Why is that? Because, Koṭṭhita, I am the one who has declared the stream-entry, the one who has declared the once-returning, the one who has declared the non-returning, the one who has declared the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, and the one who has declared the destruction of the taints. Therefore, Koṭṭhita, if anyone should say: ‘I do not acknowledge any other ascetic or brahmin who has attained the destruction of the taints,’ that would be a true statement. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, monks!
“Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:
“Here, friends, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘The noble silence, the noble silence—this is what is said.
What now is the noble silence?’”
Then, friends, it occurred to me:

“Here, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This is called noble silence.”

"Then, friends, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which is internal serenity and unification of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness.
While I was dwelling in this state, friends, perceptions and mental applications accompanied by applied thought still occurred to me.
Then, friends, the Blessed One approached me by means of his psychic power and said this:"
“‘Moggallāna, Moggallāna! Do not, brahmin, be negligent regarding noble silence;
fix the mind on noble silence; unify the mind on noble silence; concentrate the mind on noble silence.
Then, friend, after some time, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, [I attained] internal serenity...”

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal composure of mind, is free from applied and sustained thought, and is born of concentration, filled with rapture and happiness.
For if anyone, friend, speaking rightly could say:
"A disciple who is supported by the Teacher has attained great direct knowledge," it is of me that they would rightly say this.
“A disciple, favored by the Teacher, has attained great direct knowledge.
First.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 21.2 (SN 21.2, PTS SN ii 274)
1. The Chapter on Bhikkhus.
The Discourse to Upatissa.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus.
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
"In this case, friends, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind:
'Is there anything in the world such that, through its change and alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair might arise in me?'"
"Then, friends, it occurred to me:
'There is nothing in the world such that, through its change and alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair might arise in me.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, even if there were no teacher, would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise due to change and alteration?
“Friend, even if there were no teacher, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise for me; however, it would occur to me thus:
‘Alas, a teacher of great influence, of great power, and of great majesty has vanished!’”

"For if the Blessed One were to remain for a long, extended period, that would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
For indeed, in the Venerable Sāriputta, the underlying tendencies of "I-making," "mine-making," and conceit have been thoroughly uprooted for a long time.
Therefore, even because of the change and alteration of the Teacher, no sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or despair would arise in the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Second.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 21.3 (SN 21.3, PTS SN ii 275) 1.
Bhikkhuvagga (The Chapter on Monks)
The Discourse on the Jar.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, in a single dwelling.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Friend Moggallāna, your faculties are serene and the color of your face is pure and bright; surely the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna has spent today dwelling in a peaceful abiding.”
“Friends, today I dwelt in a gross abiding;
nevertheless, there was a talk on the Dhamma for me.
“But with whom, venerable Mahāmoggallāna, did you have this talk on the Dhamma?”
“Friend, I have had a Dhamma conversation with the Blessed One.
“But friend, the Blessed One is currently staying far away at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Did the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approach the Blessed One by means of psychic power?”
“Or did the Blessed One approach the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna by means of psychic power?
“I did not approach the Blessed One by means of psychic power, friend,
nor did the Blessed One approach me by means of psychic power.”
"Moreover, to the extent that the Blessed One’s divine eye and divine ear-element were purified by me,
to that same extent my divine eye and divine ear-element were purified by the Blessed One. "But in what way,
Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, did your discussion on the Dhamma with the Blessed One take place?"
“Here, friends, I said this to the Blessed One:
‘Venerable sir, it is said, “one who has aroused energy, one who has aroused energy.
In what way, venerable sir, is one called one who has aroused energy?’”
When this was said, friend, the Blessed One said this to me:
“In this case, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused:
‘Willingly, let only my skin, sinews, and bones remain, and let the flesh and blood dry up in my body, rather than I should not abandon the unwholesome state that I have not yet abandoned.’”
"That which is to be attained by human strength, human energy, and human exertion— until that has been reached, there will be no stopping of one's energy.
"In this way, Moggallāna, one is one whose energy is aroused."
"In this way, friends, did I have a Dhamma conversation with the Blessed One.
"Just as, friend, a small pebble from the Himalayas, the king of mountains, is fit only for being set aside,
even so are we to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, fit only for being set aside."
“Indeed, friend, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is of great psychic power and great majesty; were he so to wish, he could remain for an eon.
“Just as, friend, a small grain of salt would be merely a trifle compared to a large jar of salt;
even so are we a mere trifle compared to the Venerable Sāriputta.”
For the Venerable Sāriputta has been praised, extolled, and lauded by the Blessed One in many ways:
“Sāriputta alone is supreme in wisdom,
in virtue, and in tranquility.”
“Even a bhikkhu who has gone to the further shore would be no more than this.
Thus these two great nāgas rejoiced in each other’s well-spoken and well-delivered words.
The Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 21.4 (SN 21.4, PTS SN ii 277) 1.
Bhikkhu-vagga (The Chapter on Monks)
The Discourse to a New Bhikkhu. At Sāvatthī the Blessed One was staying.
Now at that time, a certain new bhikkhu, having returned from his almsround after his meal, [entered] the monastery.
Having entered, he remains inactive and silent, lounging about, and does not perform services for the bhikkhus at the time for making robes.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:

“Here, Bhante, a certain new bhikkhu, having returned from his almsround after the meal, enters his dwelling and sits about listlessly and in silence, not performing services for the bhikkhus at the time for making robes.
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, address that bhikkhu in my name, saying: ‘Friend, the Teacher calls you.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One. He then approached the other bhikkhu and said to him, “Friend, the Teacher calls you.
“Yes, friend,” that bhikkhu replied to the other bhikkhu and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As that bhikkhu was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him:

“Is it true, bhikkhu, that after returning from your almsround following the meal, you enter your dwelling and remain indolent and silent, lounging about, and do not perform services for the bhikkhus during the robe-making season?”
“Venerable sir, I too am doing my own duty.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in that bhikkhu’s mind, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, do not find fault with this bhikkhu.”
“Monks, this monk is one who gains at will, without difficulty or trouble, these four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life;
and he has, by himself, in this very world, realized that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
“Having realized the higher knowledges through direct experience and having attained them, he dwells therein.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having spoken this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
“Not by undertaking what is slack,
nor by little strength,
can nibbāna be attained.”
The liberation from all suffering.
And this young bhikkhu—
this is a supreme person.
He bears his final body,
having conquered Māra and his host. Thus ends the fourth [verse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 21.5 (SN 21.5, PTS SN ii 278) 1. Bhikkhuvagga Sujātasutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is well-born on both sides, of pure maternal and paternal descent seven generations back, unassailable and impeccable in respect of birth; when he is virtuous, mature in virtue, possessed of a guarded sense of moral shame and moral dread; when he has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and consolidates through reflection what he has learned; when he is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and belong to the higher mental states, even in this very life; when he possesses the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering—then it is fitting for him to declare: ‘I understand: Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is well-born on both sides, of pure maternal and paternal descent seven generations back, unassailable and impeccable in respect of birth; when he is virtuous, mature in virtue, possessed of a guarded sense of moral shame and moral dread; when he has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and consolidates through reflection what he has learned; when he is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and belong to the higher mental states, even in this very life; when he possesses the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering—then it is fitting for him to declare: ‘I understand: Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu come to possess the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that a bhikkhu comes to possess the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu come to possess the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, by which he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling, such its origin, such its passing away; such is perception, such its origin, such its passing away; such are volitional formations, such their origin, such their passing away; such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that a bhikkhu comes to possess the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, by which he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu come to possess the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, by which he understands as it really is: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away’ … ‘Such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away’? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The eye is impermanent; forms are impermanent; eye-consciousness is impermanent; eye-contact is impermanent; whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent. The ear is impermanent … The nose is impermanent … The tongue is impermanent … The body is impermanent … The mind is impermanent; mental phenomena are impermanent; mind-consciousness is impermanent; mind-contact is impermanent; whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that a bhikkhu comes to possess the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, by which he understands as it really is:

‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away’ … ‘Such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu come to possess the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, by which he understands as it really is: ‘The eye is impermanent; forms are impermanent; eye-consciousness is impermanent; eye-contact is impermanent; whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent’ … ‘The mind is impermanent; mental phenomena are impermanent; mind-consciousness is impermanent; mind-contact is impermanent; whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent’? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The eye is subject to arising and subject to passing away; forms are subject to arising and subject to passing away; eye-consciousness is subject to arising and subject to passing away; eye-contact is subject to arising and subject to passing away; whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to arising and subject to passing away. The ear is subject to arising and subject to passing away … The nose is subject to arising and subject to passing away … The tongue is subject to arising and subject to passing away … The body is subject to arising and subject to passing away … The mind is subject to arising and subject to passing away; mental phenomena are subject to arising and subject to passing away; mind-consciousness is subject to arising and subject to passing away; mind-contact is subject to arising and subject to passing away; whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to arising and subject to passing away. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that a bhikkhu comes to possess the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, by which he understands as it really is: ‘The eye is impermanent … that too is impermanent’ … ‘The mind is impermanent … that too is impermanent. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu come to possess the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, by which he understands as it really is: ‘The eye is subject to arising and subject to passing away; forms are subject to arising and subject to passing away; eye-consciousness is subject to arising and subject to passing away; eye-contact is subject to arising and subject to passing away; whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to arising and subject to passing away’ … ‘The mind is subject to arising and subject to passing away; mental phenomena are subject to arising and subject to passing away; mind-consciousness is subject to arising and subject to passing away; mind-contact is subject to arising and subject to passing away; whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to arising and subject to passing away’? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The eye is empty of self or of what belongs to self; forms are empty of self or of what belongs to self; eye-consciousness is empty of self or of what belongs to self; eye-contact is empty of self or of what belongs to self; whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant
He was staying at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Sujāta approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One saw the Venerable Sujāta coming from afar.
Having seen him, he addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, this clansman shines by both:
in that he is handsome, pleasing, and beautiful, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion; and for the sake of which..."

“Noble sons go forth from the home life into homelessness for the very purpose of realizing, in this very life, through their own direct knowledge, and entering upon, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life.
Thus spoke the Blessed One... [and so on].
The Teacher said:
"Truly, this bhikkhu shines forth with a mind that has become straight."
Dissociated and detached,
extinguished without clinging,
he bears his final body.
"Having conquered Māra and his host.
The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 21.6 (SN 21.6, PTS SN ii 279).
1. The Chapter on Monks (Bhikkhuvagga):
The Discourse to Bhaddiya the Dwarf (Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyasutta).
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was dwelling.
Then the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One saw the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya coming from afar;
having seen him, he addressed the monks:
“Bhikkhus, do you see this bhikkhu coming—ugly, unsightly, deformed, and treated with contempt by the bhikkhus?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“This bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is of great psychic power and great majesty; and that meditative attainment which has not yet been attained by him is not easily obtained.”

“Having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, he dwells having attained it.
Thus spoke the Blessed One...
[the Teacher].
“Swans, cranes, and peacocks,
elephants, antelopes, and deer—
all of them fear the lion.”
There is no equality in physical form.
Even so among humans,
even if one is young, if they possess wisdom;
"For in that case, it is great;
the fool is not even as much as a body.
The sixth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 21.7 (SN 21.7, PTS SN ii 280) 1. Bhikkhuvagga Visākhasutta Then the householder Visākha approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion? “There are, householder, these three things that, when developed and cultivated, lead to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. What three? The perception of unattractiveness, the perception of death, and the perception of non-delight in the entire world. These three things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. “But, venerable sir, how should the perception of unattractiveness be developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion? “Here, householder, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is how the perception of unattractiveness is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings as feelings... mind as mind... phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This too is how the perception of unattractiveness is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu reflects thus: ‘I am subject to death; I am not exempt from death. This is how the perception of death is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu reflects thus: ‘This world is not mine; I am not this world; this is not my self. This is how the perception of non-delight in the entire world is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. When this was said, the householder Visākha said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to point out the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission! “You are a lay follower, householder, one who has gone for refuge for life. It is not easy for one who still has duties to perform toward his family to receive the going forth. “Venerable sir, I have performed my duties toward my family; I have no further duties to perform toward them. “Then come, householder, and receive the going forth. Then the householder Visākha received the going forth under the Blessed One; he received the full admission. And soon, not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Visākha, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Visākha became one of the arahants. And the Venerable Visākha was one of the foremost among the arahants who were householders’ sons.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now on that occasion the Venerable Visākha Pañcāliputta was [instructing] the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk in the assembly hall.
He instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse that was polite, distinct, flawless, intelligible, comprehensive, and independent.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, who is it that, in the assembly hall, instructs, exhorts, inspires, and gladdens the bhikkhus with a discourse on the Dhamma—
using speech that is polished, clear, articulate, and expressive of the meaning?”
“Is he [teaching] that which is included within the mundane and independent?
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Visākha Pañcāliputta is in the assembly hall instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk,
using speech that is polished, clear, articulate, and unambiguous, [expressing] the meaning...”
“[It is] to be made known, included [within the world], and independent.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Visākha Pañcāliputta:
“Excellent, excellent, Visākha!”
“It is good, Visākha, that you instruct the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk... one that is relevant to the goal, connected with the meaning, and independent.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
They do not recognize a wise person who remains silent and unmixed with fools;
but they do recognize one when speaking.
Proclaiming the deathless state,
let him illuminate and clarify the Dhamma,
and raise high the banner of the Seers.
The sages have well-spoken words as their banner;
for the Dhamma is indeed the banner of the sages.
Thus ends the seventh [verse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 21.8 (SN 21.8, PTS SN ii 281) 1. Bhikkhuvagga Nanda Sutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, tantalizing; sounds cognizable by the ear... odors cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tactile objects cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, tantalizing. These are the five cords of sensual pleasure. Now, bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. It is possible that one might experience the fullness of sensual pleasures in this very life, yet not know them all fully; it is possible that one might experience the fullness of the five aggregates subject to clinging in this very life, yet not know them all fully. But it is impossible that one who has abandoned craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising, should still experience the fullness of those sensual pleasures in this very life and not know them all fully. It is impossible that one who has abandoned craving for the five aggregates subject to clinging, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising, should still experience the fullness of those five aggregates subject to clinging in this very life and not know them all fully.”
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Nanda, the son of the Blessed One’s maternal aunt, having put on robes that had been beaten and smoothed, having applied collyrium to his eyes, and having taken a bright bowl, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [stood] before the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Nanda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:

"Nanda, it is not fitting for you—a clansman who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith—to wear robes that have been beaten and smoothed, to apply collyrium to your eyes, and to carry a polished bowl."

“Nanda, it is indeed fitting for you—a clansman who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith—that you should be a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a wearer of rag-robes, and that you should dwell without regard for sensual pleasures.
Thus spoke the Blessed One... [as before] ...the Teacher.
“When shall I see Nanda,
the forest-dweller clad in rag-robes,
subsisting on gleanings from the fields?”
“...without regard for sensual pleasures.
Then, at a later time, the Venerable Nanda lived as a forest-dweller, an alms-collector, a wearer of rag-robes, and one who was without regard for sensual pleasures.
Thus ends the eighth [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 21.9 (SN 21.9, PTS SN ii 281) 1. Bhikkhuvagga Tissasutta Then the Venerable Tissa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Tissa, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is capable of achieving growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline. What five? Here, Tissa, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He is learned; he has retained in mind what he has heard, accumulated what he has heard, and consolidated what he has heard through learning; those teachings that are lovely in the beginning, lovely in the middle, and lovely in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated well by view. He is a speaker on the Dhamma; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks with loving-kindness; at the right time he speaks such words as are beneficial, reasonable, succinct, and connected with the goal. He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, Tissa, he is capable of achieving growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
[The Blessed One] was staying at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Tissa, the son of the Blessed One’s paternal aunt, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side, suffering and dejected, shedding tears. Then...
The Blessed One said this to the Venerable Tissa:
“Tissa, why are you sitting to one side, suffering and dejected, shedding tears?
“Because, Bhante, the bhikkhus have been reviling me from all sides with a shower of words,” he replied.
“However, Tissa, you are one who speaks but is not patient with what is said.
This is not fitting for you, Tissa—a clansman who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness—since you speak but are not patient with what is said.
This, rather, is fitting for you, Tissa—a clansman who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness:”
“You are one who speaks and is patient with what is spoken.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
"Why do you get angry? Do not be angry;
freedom from anger is better for you.
For it is for the sake of removing anger, conceit, and malice..."
“Tissa, the holy life is lived.
Thus it was said.
The ninth [sutta]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 21.10. (SN 21.10, PTS SN ii 282)
1. Bhikkhu-vagga, Theranāmaka-sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu named Thera was a dweller in solitude and a speaker in praise of dwelling in solitude.
He entered the village alone for alms, returned alone, sat alone in seclusion, and practiced walking meditation alone.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, a certain bhikkhu named Thera is a dweller in solitude and a speaker in praise of dwelling in solitude.
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, address the bhikkhu Thera in my name, saying:”
“The Teacher, friend elder, is summoning you.
“Very well, Bhante,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One, and he approached the Venerable Elder; having approached, he said to the Venerable Elder:
“The Teacher, friend elder, is summoning you.”
“Yes, friend,” the elder venerable one replied to that bhikkhu.
He then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As the elder venerable one was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Is it true, elder, that you dwell alone and speak in praise of dwelling alone?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“But how is it, elder, that you dwell alone and speak in praise of dwelling alone?”
“Here, Bhante, I enter a village alone for alms, I return alone, I sit in seclusion alone, and I practice walking meditation alone.
Thus, Bhante, I am one who dwells alone and I speak in praise of dwelling alone.
“There is such a thing as dwelling alone, elder; I do not say that it does not exist.”

"Moreover, elder, listen to how dwelling alone is fulfilled in detail; attend closely, and I shall speak. "Yes, venerable sir," he replied... [as before]... ...[The Blessed One said: "And what, elder, is dwelling alone? Here, elder, a bhikkhu dwells alone in a forest, at the foot of a tree, in an empty hut, in a mountain glen, in a rocky cave, in a charnel ground, in the open air, or on a heap of straw. This is called dwelling alone. "And what, elder, is dwelling in seclusion? Here, elder, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him. Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Abandoning ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Abandoning sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor. Abandoning restlessness and remorse, he dwells without agitation, with a mind inwardly peaceful; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt, he dwells having gone beyond doubt, unperplexed about wholesome qualities; he purifies his mind from doubt. "When, elder, these five hindrances have been abandoned within him, he sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering’; he sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. "And what, elder, is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the way leading to the cessation of suffering. "When, elder, a bhikkhu has developed and cultivated this Noble Eightfold Path, he understands as it really is the meaning of these things; he penetrates them with wisdom and sees them by means of the higher wisdom. This is called dwelling in seclusion. "And what, elder, is the development of the four foundations of mindfulness? Here, elder, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called the development of the four foundations of mindfulness. "And what, elder, is the development of the four right strivings? Here, elder, a bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states... He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states... He generates desire for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states, for their non-decline, increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. This is called the development of the four right strivings. "And what, elder, is the development of the four bases for psychic power? Here, elder, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind... concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. This is called the development of the four bases for psychic power. "And what, elder, is the development of the five spiritual faculties? Here, elder, a bhikkhu develops the faculty of faith, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release; he develops the faculty of energy... the faculty of mindfulness... the faculty of concentration... the faculty of wisdom, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. This is called the development of the five spiritual faculties. "And what, elder, is the development of the five powers? Here, elder, a bhikkhu develops the power of faith... the power of energy... the power of mindfulness... the power of concentration... the power of wisdom, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. This is called the development of the five powers. "And what, elder, is the development of the seven factors of enlightenment? Here, elder, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release; he develops the enlightenment factor of discrimination of phenomena... the enlightenment factor of energy... the enlightenment factor of rapture... the enlightenment factor of tranquility... the enlightenment factor of concentration... the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. This is called the development of the seven factors of enlightenment. "And what, elder, is the development of the Noble Eightfold Path? Here, elder, a bhikkhu develops right view... right intention... right speech... right action... right livelihood... right effort... right mindfulness... right concentration, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. This is called the development of the Noble Eightfold Path. "It is in this way, elder, that dwelling alone is fulfilled in detail. "So it is, Blessed One," he replied. The Blessed One then rose from his seat and departed. The Venerable Sāriputta then addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus!"—"Friend! those bhikkhus replied. The Venerable Sāriputta said this: "Friends, the Blessed One has taught me this Dhamma discourse on dwelling alone in detail. As I understood the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, as soon as I had mastered it, I attained final Nibbāna in this very life. "Indeed, friend, the Venerable Sāriputta is wise; indeed, friend, the Venerable Sāriputta has great wisdom! For the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna in this very life, having mastered this Dhamma discourse on dwelling alone taught by the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus!"—"Friend! those bhikkhus replied. The Venerable Ānanda said this: "Friends, the Blessed One has taught me this Dhamma discourse on dwelling alone in detail. As I understood the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, as soon as I had mastered it, I attained final Nibbāna in this very life. "Indeed, friend, the Venerable Ānanda is wise; indeed, friend, the Venerable Ānanda has great wisdom! For the Venerable Ānanda has attained final Nibbāna in this very life, having mastered this Dhamma discourse on dwelling alone taught by the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus!"—"Friend! those bhikkhus replied. The Venerable Sāriputta said this: "Friends, the Blessed One has taught me this Dhamma discourse on dwelling alone in detail. As I understood the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, as soon as I had mastered it, I attained final Nibbāna in this very life. "Indeed, friend, the Venerable Sāriputta is wise; indeed, friend, the Venerable Sāriputta has great wisdom! For the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna in this very life, having mastered this Dhamma discourse on dwelling alone taught by the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus!"—"Friend! those bhikkhus replied. The Venerable Ānanda said this: "Friends, the Blessed One has taught me this Dhamma discourse on dwelling alone in detail. As I understood the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, as soon as I had mastered it, I attained final Nibbāna in this very life. "Indeed, friend, the Venerable Ānanda is wise; indeed, friend, the Venerable Ānanda has great wisdom! For the Venerable Ānanda has attained final Nibbāna in this very life, having mastered this Dhamma discourse on dwelling alone taught by the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus!"—"Friend! those bhikk
“And how, elder, is dwelling alone fulfilled in detail?
Here, elder, what is past is abandoned; what is future is relinquished; and with regard to the acquisition of individuality in the present, desire and lust are thoroughly removed.
It is in this way, elder, that dwelling alone is fulfilled in detail.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
“The All-Conqueror, the All-Knower, the Wise One—”
“Untainted by all phenomena, having abandoned everything,
liberated through the destruction of craving—
I call that person one who dwells alone.”
The Tenth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 21.11 (SN 21.11, PTS SN ii 284) 1.
Bhikkhu-vagga (The Chapter on Monks)
The Mahākappina Sutta.
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Mahākappina approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One saw the Venerable Mahākappina coming from afar.
Having seen him, he addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, do you see that bhikkhu coming—pale, thin, and with a prominent nose?"
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Indeed, monks, this monk is of great psychic power and great majesty.
And there is no attainment that is easily won which has not previously been attained by that monk.”

“Having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, he dwells having attained it.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
“The Kshatriya is the best among those people who rely on lineage;
but one endowed with true knowledge and conduct— ”
He is the best among gods and humans.
By day the sun shines,
and by night the moon radiates light.
The kṣatriya shines when he is girt for battle;
the brahmin shines when he is meditating;
but then, throughout the entire day and night, [the ascetic shines].
“The Buddha shines with splendor.
Thus ends the eleventh [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 21.12 (SN 21.12, PTS SN ii 285).
1. Bhikkhuvagga Sahāyakasutta.
At Sāvatthī he was staying.
Then two monks who were friends and had been the personal attendants (*saddhivihārin*) of the Venerable Mahākappina approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One saw those monks coming from afar.
Having seen them, he addressed the monks:
“Bhikkhus, do you see those bhikkhus coming, companions and co-residents of Kappina?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”—
“These indeed are bhikkhus of great psychic power and great majesty.”
"And there is no attainment that was not previously attained by those bhikkhus,

for they have entered and dwell, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then spoke further:
“These monks have been companions for a long time, having lived together for many years.”
Their true Dhamma accords with the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha;
they are well-trained by Kappina.
In the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble One,
they bear their final body,
having conquered Māra and his host.
The twelfth.
The first section on monks.
Its summary verse:
Kolita and Upatissa,
and also Ghaṭa;
Nava, Sujāta, and Bhaddi.
Visākha, Nanda, and Tissa;
and the Elder named Kappina,
together with his companion— these are twelve.
The Saṃyutta Nikāya on the Bhikkhus is finished.
This is the second chapter, the Nidāna-vagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
The Chapter on the Realization of the Causes,
the Chapter on the Beginningless, the Chapter on Kassapa,
the Chapter on Honors, the Chapter on Rāhula, and the Chapter on Characteristics.
The Chapter on Similes is concluded;
thus it is called the second.
The Pāḷi of the Nidāna Vagga Saṃyutta is finished.
